app_claim: Hadrian’s Wall [122 → 410]: “The north-west frontier of the Roman empire for nearly 300 years … It was given up about AD 142 when the frontier moved north to the Antonine Wall, and reoccupied some twenty years later.” The app’s uncertainty adds, “The break in use about 142-160 is not shown.”
problem: The single continuous visible interval presents the Wall as the active north-west frontier throughout c142-160, even though its own text places the frontier on the Antonine Wall then. English Heritage says Antoninus Pius abandoned Hadrian’s Wall and moved the frontier to the Forth–Clyde isthmus, returning later; English Heritage’s fort pages qualify this as incomplete abandonment or reduced caretaker garrisons. The continuous geometry is defensible for the physical monument, but the “frontier … for nearly 300 years” wording and unbroken active display are misleading.

evidence.title: History of Hadrian’s Wall
evidence.what_it_says: Hadrian’s Wall was built from AD 122; Antoninus Pius “abandoned Hadrian’s Wall and moved the frontier” to the Antonine Wall, which had a short life of about 20 years before return to Hadrian’s Wall, when it was brought back into working order.

evidence.title: History of Housesteads Roman Fort
evidence.what_it_says: The Antonine Wall was abandoned after AD 160 and Hadrian’s Wall fully garrisoned; it is often thought Hadrian’s Wall was abandoned c142, but excavations found no evidence at Housesteads and part of the garrison may have remained.

new_values.$[31].summary: The north-west frontier of the Roman empire from the Tyne to the Solway, built by the army on Hadrian’s orders after his visit in AD 122. The physical wall remained visible, but the active frontier moved to the Antonine Wall about AD 142; some forts may have kept reduced garrisons before Hadrian’s Wall was fully recommissioned by about AD 160.
new_values.$[31].uncertainty: Course: drawn through the positions of the sixteen forts from Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway, placed from general knowledge, so the line cuts corners between forts by up to a kilometre. The whole wall lies inside the map. The single line intentionally shows the physical monument continuously; the c142-c160 shift of the active frontier to the Antonine Wall and partial recommissioning are not modelled as a separate phase. The end date is nominal: garrisons stayed into the early 5th century and some forts were occupied later.

app_claim: Great North Road (London–York–Berwick) [1200 → present]. “The main medieval road from London to the north, by Barnet, Hatfield, Baldock …” Its uncertainty says, “The name is post-medieval. In the Middle Ages the route out of London by Ware, Royston and Huntingdon (the Old North Road) was more important.”
problem: The drawn Barnet–Hatfield–Stevenage–Baldock line is shown as the “main medieval road” from 1200, but its own note concedes that the principal medieval route was the Old North Road via Ware, Royston and Huntingdon. Hertfordshire’s Historic Environment Record says the Hatfield stretch of the Great North Road was “essentially pieced together in the 16th century from local roads”; Baldock’s local history distinguishes the medieval route via Ware from the later route via Stevenage/Baldock and dates the “Great North Road” label to the turnpike era. The visible feature therefore places a post-medieval alignment and name about four centuries too early.

evidence.title: Old Course Of The Great North Road, Hatfield Park, Hatfield
evidence.publisher: Historic England Heritage Gateway / Hertfordshire HER
evidence.what_it_says: The 1784–1851 course of the turnpike road through Hatfield Park; the HER states that the Great North Road there was “essentially pieced together in the 16th century from local roads.”

evidence.title: The Road to London (Baldock history article)
evidence.publisher: Baldock Museum and Local History Society
evidence.what_it_says: Medieval Baldock travellers went to London via Walkern and Ware; the later Baldock–Stevenage route was described in 1575 as a common highway and the road was known as the Great North Road after the 1720 Turnpike Trust.

evidence.title: Route of the Great North Road
evidence.what_it_says: The classic Great North Road route out of London via Hatfield, Stevenage and Baldock displaced the earlier Old North Road via Royston; the early medieval route was more westerly and by the 14th century returned toward Ermine Street through Grantham, Newark and Doncaster.

new_values.$[40].name: Great North Road (London–York–Berwick; later route)
new_values.$[40].summary: The post-medieval road from London to the north, assembled in the 16th century from local roads and later the classic coaching route by Barnet, Hatfield, Baldock, Stamford, Grantham, Newark, Doncaster, Boroughbridge, Durham and Newcastle to Berwick. It replaced the older medieval London route via Ware, Royston and Huntingdon as long-distance travel shifted westward.
new_values.$[40].uncertainty: Course: straight segments between the towns on the route, placed from general knowledge; no source was fetched for the exact geometry. The 1600 start is nominal: the Hatfield HER says the road was pieced together in the 16th century, while the name “Great North Road” is later and is securely associated with the turnpike/coaching era. The medieval main route out of London was the Old North Road via Ware, Royston and Huntingdon and is not shown by this geometry. York was reached by a branch from near Wetherby or Ferrybridge.

app_claim: The sea-level keyframes run from -6.0 m in 4000 BCE to -0.25 m in 1625. The note says they are “one relative sea-level curve … for the Thames / Fenland / Hampshire-Sussex-Kent region” and that “north of a line roughly from the Mersey to the Tees this curve drowns too little or shows the wrong sign; apply it at full strength only south of about 53.5 N.” The engine’s seaLevel(t) returns one interpolated scalar for the whole map and passes it to the national terrain shader.
problem: A southern relative sea-level curve is being applied to the whole national map. The dataset’s own note concedes that at 4000 BCE Northumberland relative sea level was about +1.5 m and the Solway +2 to +4 m, while the model applies -6 m. This visibly drowns too little and shows the wrong sign on northern coasts. Shennan, Bradley and Edwards’s database paper records radically different relative sea-level histories across Britain and Ireland because of glacio-isostatic adjustment; it does not support one national scalar.

evidence.title: Relative sea-level changes and crustal movements in Britain and Ireland since the Last Glacial Maximum
evidence.what_it_says: The paper describes a >2,100-point sea-level database across 86 regions and “radically different patterns” of relative sea-level change between northern and southern Britain, driven by glacio-isostatic response to the Celtic Ice Sheet.

evidence.title: Data for: Relative sea-level changes and crustal movements in Britain and Ireland since the Last Glacial Maximum
evidence.what_it_says: Publishes the underlying database of sea-level index points for Britain and Ireland.

app_claim: Kingdom of the Northumbrians [654 → 867]. “York fell to the Great Army in 867.” The later Earldom of Northumbria starts only in 954. Between those dates no Northumbrian polity is shown north of the Tees/Tyne.
problem: Ending the Northumbrian polity in 867 implies that the kingdom disappeared when York fell. It did not. Viking rulers took York and southern Deira, while Bamburgh-based rulers retained northern Northumbria, later as high-reeves or earls under West Saxon suzerainty, until 954. The current dataset already shows the southern Viking Kingdom of York separately, so leaving the northern rump blank creates a nearly century-long gap.

evidence.title: The Kingdom Of Northumbria
evidence.what_it_says: Northumbrian kings ruled Bernicia and Deira until the Viking conquest of the 860s-870s; thereafter Scandinavian rulers held York and the south, while “a line of independent earls ruled the north from Bamburgh, eventually under West Saxon suzerainty.”

evidence.title: Earl of Northumbria
evidence.what_it_says: After 867, southern Northumbria became the Viking Kingdom of York, while the rulers of Bamburgh commanded territory north of the Tees; Scandinavian domination ended in 954 and the whole area was then governed by earls.

new_values.$[34].name: Northumbria: kingdom, Bamburgh rulers and earldom
new_values.$[34].summary: Bernicia and Deira united under Oswiu. After Viking York took Deira in 867, the northern rump continued under Bamburgh rulers/high-reeves; after 954 the whole area was governed as an earldom under English kings. This is a continuous northern polity, with southern Viking York shown separately.

app_claim: The woodland trend says: “The trend is for England; Wales was more wooded at most dates.” The engine’s woodland(t) returns one interpolated scalar for the whole national map and passes it to the terrain shader.
problem: The dataset explicitly describes a national viewer but supplies an England-only woodland trend and applies it to Wales too. This understates Welsh woodland cover at most dates. Rackham’s work also emphasizes uneven regional woodland distribution, not a single national percentage.

evidence.title: Forest and upland
evidence.what_it_says: Rackham’s chapter states that Anglo-Saxon England was unevenly wooded and that Domesday woodland was distributed in distinct regional concentrations.

evidence.title: British forest landscapes: the legacy of woodland fragmentation
evidence.what_it_says: Modern national inventory data show woodland cover as 8.4% in England and 13.8% in Wales, illustrating that England and Wales differ materially.

location: The Ridgeway / Berkshire Downs and Chilterns
app_claim: The Ridgeway [from -3000] with evidence class `conjectural` and confidence `low`: “The chalk ridge route from the Avebury area along the Berkshire Downs to the Thames at Goring, and on along the Chiltern scarp (as the Icknield Way) to Ivinghoe Beacon…” Its note adds, “That a single long-distance prehistoric road existed here is an old idea that archaeologists now doubt…”
problem: The feature’s geometry is the modern National Trail, but the data begins it at 3000 BCE and gives a continuous long-distance route. Archaeological work summarized by Sarah Harrison shows the Icknield Way/Ridgeway concept is problematic; excavations indicate the line in some places was not open in the Bronze or Iron Ages and that the earliest firm evidence for a way is in 10th-century charters. Since the app already calls the idea conjectural, using a visible start date of 3000 BCE overstates the certainty and turns a modern trail into an ancient continuous routeway.

evidence.title: The Icknield Way: Some Queries
evidence.what_it_says: The article argues that the assumptions about the Icknield Way’s date, origins and whereabouts are essentially erroneous, based on historiographical myth and failure to keep up with changing ideas about prehistoric societies.

evidence.title: The Ridgeway between Avebury and Overton Downs
evidence.what_it_says: The landscape on Overton and Fyfield Downs contains prehistoric field systems; the Ridgeway as currently defined is later than these systems and cannot be shown to have existed continuously from the 2nd or 1st millennium BCE.

evidence.title: The Ridgeway and the Icknield Way: history
evidence.what_it_says: The National Trail was designated in 1972 and opened in 1973; the ancient Ridgeway is a loose band of parallel tracks, and the earliest documentary evidence for the Icknield Way in this area is a 10th-century charter reference to `Icenhilde weg`.

new_values.$[39].name: Ridgeway / Icknield Way: possible later prehistoric corridor
new_values.$[39].summary: A possible long-distance corridor along the chalk ridge from Avebury via the Berkshire Downs to the Thames at Goring and onward through the Chilterns to Ivinghoe Beacon. The drawn line is the modern National Trail, not a proved prehistoric road.
new_values.$[39].uncertainty: This is a conjectural composite of later tracks and modern paths. Archaeologists now doubt a single continuous prehistoric Icknield Way; the earliest firm documentary evidence in this area is 10th-century charters calling an `Icenhilde weg`. The 900 CE start is a deliberately conservative date for a way that can be securely named, not a claim that the whole modern trail existed then.
